Subject: Printer quote: need to decide by Friday the 21st

Hi all,

I just got off the call with Dana at the printer. Here is where things stand.

The price goes up 12% from the spring issue, from $4,200 to about $4,700 a run. Dana said they will hold the old price if we sign a two-year contract. Either way, turnaround drops from 10 working days to 7.

For comparison, the other quote we got last year was $5,100, so even the higher price is below that.

I lean toward signing the two-year deal, since it keeps the cost where it is and the faster turnaround comes regardless. Before I answer Dana, though, I want to hear objections. If you see a reason not to commit for two years, tell me. They need an answer by Friday the 21st.

Thanks,
Alex

It was scheduled for 9:00 and went out at 2:40 in the afternoon. The mailing tool refused to send because the list I imported had about 300 duplicate addresses. I didn't find out until 11, when someone asked where it was, and cleaning the list took the rest of the time. That one's on me. From now on I'll check the import the day before. The open rate looks normal anyway: 41%, against the usual 43%.

Subject: Last Thursday's workshop: what happened and what changes

Hi everyone,

Last Thursday's public workshop was overbooked. We had 60 seats and 78 people turned up, and 18 of them stood or left.

The cause was the sign-up form. The limit of 60 was set on the old form, not on the copy we made in March, so the copy stayed open past the limit.

Four people complained by email. Each got an apology and a free place at the next workshop, which is on the 14th.

To keep this from happening again, one named person will own each event's form and close it by hand. The job rotates, so you may be asked to take a turn. If your name is on an event, the form is yours until that event is over, and closing it is part of the job.

Thanks for your patience while we fix this.

Alex

Subject: Review request: rewritten "How to request time off" page

Hi,

I rewrote the "How to request time off" page and need your approval before it replaces the old one.

What changed:
- The page is now about 500 words, down from 1,400.
- The step-by-step instructions are at the top.
- The paper form section is gone. The paper form was retired in 2023.
- New section: what to do when your manager is away. Ask their deputy, who is listed in the staff directory.

The policy itself did not change, only the wording and the order.

One thing I'd like you to look at in particular: I wasn't sure whether "at least two weeks' notice" applies to single days off, so I kept the old wording. If you know the answer, tell me and I'll update it.

Thanks,
Alex

Subject: Your grant report

Hi,

Thanks for thinking of me. I'm sorry, but I can't edit the full report by Monday, because I'm on deadline for the annual report until Wednesday.

Here is what I can do. By Monday I could read the summary and the budget narrative, about 6 pages. Or I could do the whole report by the Friday after.

If neither works, Priya, a freelancer I trust, may have time this week. I'm happy to point you to her.

I know the grant pays for two positions, so I want the report to go well, whichever way we do it. Let me know which option suits you.

Alex

Subject: Website rewrite: weekly update

Hi,

Short version: the rewrite is moving, but the services pages could cost us a week.

Progress
- 34 of 52 pages are rewritten, up from 27 last week.
- The About section is finished and signed off.
- The photo shoot is booked for Tuesday.

Stuck
- The services pages. Legal has had the pricing language for 9 days, and I have chased twice.

Risk
If legal has not answered by Thursday, the launch on the 30th slips by a week.

I need nothing from you, except perhaps a nudge to legal if you are able to give one.

Alex

- The news is buried. The library opens on May 3, but that doesn't show up until the third paragraph, and the first paragraph is all background. Move the opening date to the top.
- It runs 600 words. Aim for about 350.
- The director's quote is good, so keep it.

Fix the order and the length and it's ready for another look.

Your Meeting Notes Are Not Helping Anyone

A 90-minute planning meeting produces four pages of notes. Afterward, nobody can say who owns the budget. Four pages, and the one fact the team needed is not in them.

That is the problem with most meeting notes. They record what was said, not what was decided. A running account tells you who raised which concern and in what order, which is useful to no one the following Tuesday. Whoever opens them later has to dig through the discussion to find out where it ended up. Nobody reads these documents after two days. They go into a folder and stay there.

The part worth keeping fits in three lines. What was decided. Who does what by when. What is still open. If you can write those, you have captured the meeting. If you can't, that is worth knowing too, because it means the meeting did not finish its job.

So why do we keep writing long notes? Because they feel diligent. A thorough document looks like work, and the person who wrote it looks careful. Length signals effort, and effort is easy to confuse with usefulness. Nobody gets criticized for being too thorough, so the habit survives.

But thoroughness aimed at the wrong target is just volume. Notes should help people act, not prove that someone was paying attention. The next time you are handed the job of taking notes, try writing the three lines first. Put them at the top. If anything else seems worth keeping, add it underneath, where nobody is forced to read it.

Subject: Volunteer handbook: review needed by Wednesday the 12th

Hi all,

The new volunteer handbook draft is finished. It runs 22 pages, and the old one was last updated in 2021, so a lot has changed.

I need your review, especially of section 3 (safeguarding) and section 5 (shift scheduling). Even a careful read of just those two sections would help a great deal. Please put comments in the shared document by Wednesday the 12th. Printing is booked for the 17th, so later changes cannot go in.

I know it is a busy month for you. If it is easier, I can walk anyone through the changes in 15 minutes, so you would not need to read all 22 pages cold.

Thank you,
Alex

Subject: Planning meeting: what we decided

Hi everyone,

Thanks for your time at Tuesday's planning meeting. It ran 90 minutes, so I have kept this to the decisions only. Please check that your name and date are right.

The autumn campaign launches on October 6, not September 15. The budget stays at 40,000, but 6,000 moves from print ads to video.

Two people own next steps. Sam owns the video brief, due on the 20th. Lena owns the mailing list cleanup, due at the end of the month.

One question is still open: whether to hire a freelance designer. We did not decide it. Omar will get two quotes by Friday.

The next meeting is on the 27th. If anything here does not match your memory of the meeting, reply and tell me.

Alex

Don't Borrow Your Process From a Company of Thousands

Big companies add process for a reason. When hundreds of people who do not know each other have to work together, someone needs to write things down, sign things off, and plan a quarter ahead. Process is how strangers coordinate.

A team of six is not in that position. You already know what everyone is doing. You hear it across the room or in a quick message. The coordination problem that process solves is mostly not yours.

But the habits are easy to copy: weekly status reports, approval chains, quarterly planning documents. They look like what a serious organization does. The trouble is that they cost the same hours in a small team and return less.

Take a five-person shop that spent every Monday morning writing status reports nobody read. Each of the five already knew what the others were up to. The reports ate the start of every week and told no one anything new.

What a small team needs is simpler. Keep a shared list of what is in progress, so anyone can see the state of things at a glance. And keep the habit of talking to each other, which no document replaces.

This is not an argument against process forever. Add it when something has broken twice, not before. Until then, don't pay for coordination you don't need.

Subject: Request to move our June booking to a larger room

Dear events manager,

I'm writing about our members' evening, which is booked for Thursday 12 June. I'd like to move it to Thursday 19 June. Our expected numbers have also grown from 80 to about 110, so we will need a larger room.

Could you tell me whether the larger room is free on the 19th, and what it would cost? The $600 deposit is already paid, and the catering stays the same.

Our invitations go to print on Monday, so I need an answer by Friday. If you can let me know sooner, that would be a great help.

Thank you,
Alex

Subject: Annual report status

Hi,

Here is where the annual report stands, in short: most of it is moving, and two items are waiting on other people.

The text went to the designer on Monday, and 3 of the 5 sections are laid out. The finance pages are waiting for the audited figures, which are due on the 14th. The chair's foreword came in 400 words too long, so I'm cutting it now. The print deadline of the 28th still holds.

One thing I need from you: please pick the cover photo by Wednesday. There are two options to choose from, and I'd like your decision by then so nothing else has to wait on it.

Thanks,
Alex

Subject: Your March invoice was paid twice

Hi,

I'm writing to let you know that we paid your March invoice for $1,850 twice. The mistake was on our side: it was entered once from the emailed copy and once from the copy that came by post.

You can either refund the extra payment, or we can take it off your April invoice, which hasn't arrived yet. We would prefer to take it off April, if that works for you.

I'm sorry for the trouble. Finance now logs invoices by invoice number, so this should not happen again.

Best,
Alex

Thanks for covering the library grant press release while I'm out Thursday and Friday. The release is drafted and just waiting on a quote from the director. She's promised it by Thursday noon. Once it's in, send the release to the usual list of 42 contacts. The embargo is Friday at 9:00. The photo is in the shared folder under "grant". If the quote doesn't come, send the release without it rather than miss the embargo.

Subject: Expense claims are moving online

Hi everyone,

Expense claims are moving from paper forms to an online form. The online form replaces paper from the 1st of next month, and we will still accept paper claims until the 15th.

A few things to know:
- Photograph your receipts and attach them to the form.
- A claim over $200 still needs your manager's sign-off first.
- Payments will now go out every second Friday, where they used to go out monthly.

If you would like to see how it works, there is a 20-minute walkthrough on Tuesday at 1:00.

Thanks,
Alex

Subject: Re: Saturday's family tour

Hello,

Thank you for writing, and I'm sorry about Saturday's family tour. You should have been told it was cancelled, and you weren't.

Our guide called in sick at 8:15, for a tour that was due to start at 10:00. We sent a cancellation email at 8:40, but it only went to people who had booked online. You had booked by phone, as had five other families, so none of you heard from us. That was our failure.

We are refunding your $18, and we would like to offer you a free place on any tour this season. From now on, phone bookings get a text message as well.

Again, I'm sorry for the disappointment.

Sincerely,
Alex

Subject: Stock-photo subscription recommendation

Hi,

I recommend we cancel the stock-photo subscription and book two photographer days instead.

The subscription costs $1,100 a year and renews on the 30th. Last year the team used 23 images from it, and one person used 17 of them. Free image libraries covered most of what we needed. A day with the staff photographer costs $450 and gave us 60 usable images last time, so two days would cost $900, less than the subscription.

The one risk is a last-minute need with no photo to hand. I think that is worth accepting.

Since it renews on the 30th, I'd need your decision before then.

Alex

Subject: Decision needed on 12 June: new membership database

Dear board members,

I'm asking the board to approve a replacement for our membership database at the meeting on 12 June.

The contract for the current system ends on 31 August, and it costs $5,800 a year. We collected three quotes, at $6,400, $7,900 and $9,200 a year. I recommend the $7,900 option, because it imports our existing records and includes staff training. The cheapest one has no event booking.

Moving the records takes about three weeks, so a decision on 12 June leaves enough time before the current contract ends on 31 August.

The three quotes are the basis for this request, and I'm happy to go through any of them in more detail before the meeting. Please let me know if you have any questions, and I will be glad to answer them.

Thank you,
Alex

Short version: 1,500 of the 2,000 leaflets arrived. The printer ran out of the paper stock, and the other 500 arrive on Wednesday, so we still have time before the open day on Saturday. They took 10% off the invoice. One catch: about 200 of the delivered leaflets have a smudge on the back page. They're fine for internal use but not for handing out, so I'd keep those away from the open day.

Subject: Summer program sign-ups, weekly update

Hi,

Sign-ups are at 212 so far, against our target of 300. We had 61 this week, up from 38 last week.

Most of this week's sign-ups came from school visits: visits to three schools brought in 44. The paid social ads cost $380 and brought in 9. I propose we stop the ads and visit two more schools instead.

Timing matters here, because the early-bird price ends on the 20th, so the school visits are worth starting soon. Separately, the pottery class has a waiting list of 14.

Let me know if you are happy for me to go ahead with that change, or if you would like to talk it through first.

Thanks,
Alex

Subject: Donation page outage: what happened and what we changed

Hi everyone,

Over the weekend our donation page stopped taking payments. It took none from Sunday at 6:00 in the evening until Monday at 9:30 in the morning.

The cause was a lapsed account with our payment service. The renewal notice went to a former colleague's email address, so nobody here saw it.

About 40 people tried to donate during that time, and 12 of them emailed us. Everyone who emailed has been contacted. The gifts that did not go through come to an estimated $2,300.

To stop this happening again, renewal notices now go to a shared inbox, and a calendar reminder is set 30 days ahead of each renewal.

I'm sorry for the disruption, and thank you to everyone who helped follow up with donors.

Alex

Subject: Communications folder reorganization, for your approval

Hi,

I've reorganized the Communications folder on the shared drive and would like your approval before I announce it. Here is what changed, so you can review it quickly.

The folder holds about 1,900 files. It went from 46 top-level folders to 7. Nothing was deleted: the old structure is archived read-only for three months. File names now start with the date, then the project, and all templates are in one folder. I also updated 11 links in the staff handbook.

I plan to announce it on Friday, once you have signed off. Before then, could you please check two things: the seven folder names, and the archive plan?

Thanks,
Alex

The first day decides

Most volunteers who leave do it early. The majority go within their first month, long before anything could wear down their belief in the cause.

When you ask them why, the cause rarely comes up. They tell you they did not know what to do. Nobody seemed to expect them. No task was ready when they arrived. That is not a story about people who stopped caring. It is a story about a first day that gave their care nowhere to go.

So if you run a volunteer program, the thing to fix is probably not motivation. It is the first shift. A good one is not complicated: a named person to meet, one real task, and a thank-you at the end.

Pairing helps too. One food bank gave each new volunteer a buddy for their first two shifts. Its first-month drop-out fell from about half to about a quarter. The cause had not changed. The only difference was that people had someone waiting for them and something to do.

There is a practical reason to care as well. Recruiting a new volunteer costs more time than keeping one. Every person who walks out after a bad first day is a person you will have to find all over again.
